title: Present perfect or past simple?
tagline: One question decides it: does the sentence say exactly when?
why: Two tenses, one big decision: does the sentence give a finished time (yesterday, in 2020, two days ago) or not (ever, for, since, this week)? Cambridge tests this constantly — in Reading Part 6 you choose the right form, and in Speaking you might say I've lived in Lima for five years, but I moved here in 2019. Mixing them up is the most common tense mistake at this level.

hook.text: Sofia and Liam are talking about Lima. "I've lived here since 2015," says Sofia. "I moved here in 2022," says Liam. "Have you ever visited the Plaza Mayor?" "Yes, I went there last month."
hook.ask: One sentence gives a finished time; the other doesn't. Can you find the present perfect and the past simple, and say which time word goes with each?

diagrams.title: Finished, or still true?

marks.label: both are still in Lima now

diagrams.caption: Past simple = the action is finished and in the past. Present perfect = the situation started in the past and is still true now.

diagrams.title: Same idea, two different tenses
diagrams.caption: The time word decides the tense: in 2022, last month → past simple. since 2015, no exact time → present perfect.

examples.note: last year = finished time → past simple
in + a past year = finished time
ago = a finished point in the past

use.point: No exact time, or an experience → present perfect

examples.note: no exact date, just an experience

examples.text: Have you ever been to the Plaza Mayor?
examples.note: ever = at any time in your life
no exact time, close to now

use.point: for and since — how long a situation has continued

examples.text: I've lived in Lima for ten years.

examples.note: How long…? asks for a length of time

use.point: Unfinished time — this week, today, this month

examples.note: this week isn't over yet → present perfect
this month is still happening → present perfect

watch_out.wrong: I have visited Cusco last year.
watch_out.why: Last year is a finished time word — it needs the past simple, never the present perfect.
Since always needs the present perfect, because the situation is still true now.

watch_out.wrong: How long you have lived here?
watch_out.why: In a question, have/has moves before the person.
Yesterday tells you exactly when — that always means past simple.

watch_out.wrong: I live here for ten years.
watch_out.right: I've lived here for ten years.
watch_out.why: A situation that started in the past and continues now needs the present perfect, not the present simple.

l1.wrong: I have visited Cusco last year.
l1.why: 'El año pasado' is a finished time — English needs the past simple, not the present perfect that Spanish sometimes suggests.
Spanish uses the present (vivo) for a situation that continues; English uses the present perfect with since.

l1.wrong: How much time you live here?
l1.why: This question always uses How long + present perfect in English, not How much time + the present.
For an experience at no exact time, English prefers the present perfect with never/ever, not the past simple.

remember.trick: A date = past simple. No date or 'since' = present perfect.
remember.tip: Ask yourself: does the sentence say exactly when? Yes → past simple. Not sure, or still true now? → present perfect.

can_do: I can choose past simple for a finished time (yesterday, in 2020, ago) and present perfect for no exact time (ever, just, already).
I can use for and since to say how long a situation has continued.
I can ask and answer How long have you…?
summary: A finished time word (yesterday, last week, in 2020, ago) always needs the past simple.
No exact time, or an experience in your life (ever, never, just, already) needs the present perfect.
For + a length of time, since + a starting point — both with the present perfect, for a situation that continues now.
This week, today and this month can go with either tense, depending on whether they're finished or not.
Ask yourself: does the sentence say exactly when? Yes → past simple. Not sure, or still true now? → present perfect.
